function_question: How does nature make surfaces slippery?

opening.text: There was a boy called Zane who loved Friday nights, because Friday was family burger night.
Zane counted down to Friday and made sure the table was ready: buns, plates and the big red ketchup bottle.
The bottle was nearly empty. Zane shook it and squeezed it, but the last bit clung to the sides. "There's loads left in there," he said. "Why won't it come out?"

card.problem: The last ketchup stays stuck in the bottle
card.goal: A surface that sticky stuff slides right off
card.rules: Test with a teaspoon of ketchup over 20 cm

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: The stubborn bottle
chapters.line: Zane wonders: what if ketchup could slide out like water?

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: Zane needs a sidekick
chapters.line: Burger night needs two problem-solvers. Will you join Zane?

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: The nature heroes
chapters.line: You and Zane meet heroes that nothing can stick to.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: The secret of the slippery layer
chapters.line: The heroes reveal the thin layer that makes everything slide.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: The drop-race ramp
chapters.line: Zane props a tray on two books and grabs a stopwatch.

chapters.label: Chapter 5½
chapters.title: Kind, useful feedback
chapters.line: You learn three magic sentence starters for making any idea better.

chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: The plan
chapters.line: Every great surface starts as a close-up drawing.

chapters.label: Chapter 7
chapters.title: The big slide
chapters.line: The first blob creeps slowly. You get feedback, fix it, and it races down.

chapters.label: Chapter 8
chapters.title: Not a drop wasted
chapters.line: The ketchup slides out, and burger night is saved.

guide.brief: I'm Popi, your story guide. At Zane's burger night, the last bit of ketchup always stays stuck in the bottle. Can you help him make it slide right out? Let's start!
guide.your_idea: Some designers already have a slippery idea up their sleeve. Do you?
guide.nature_clues: Nature was making slippery surfaces long before ketchup was invented. Tap each card to meet four heroes nothing can stick to!
guide.design_secret: Here's the secret all four heroes share…
guide.skill: Scientists predict before they test. Which surface will make the ketchup win the race? Don't eat the test ketchup!
guide.sketch: Time to draw your surface up close, like a real materials scientist!
guide.build_and_test: Build your slippery ramp and race a teaspoon of ketchup 20 cm. How many seconds does it take?
guide.retry_tip: Ask for an I like, an I wish and a What if. Then change just ONE thing and race again!
guide.ending: And ever since then, Zane's family never wastes a drop, and every Friday the ketchup slides out as smooth as a snail.

quick_check.question: Zane's ketchup slides 20 cm in 4 seconds. How many centimetres does it slide each second?
quick_check.right: Right! 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm every second. That's a speedy blob!
quick_check.wrong: Not quite. Share the 20 cm equally between the 4 seconds: 20 ÷ 4.

clue_cards.name: Pitcher plant
clue_cards.trick: Tiny ridges on its rim hold a thin film of water.
clue_cards.does: Insects slip on the wet rim like cars on a wet road.

clue_cards.name: Snail
clue_cards.trick: It makes a thin, wet layer of slime under its foot.
clue_cards.does: The slime lets it slide over rough stones and sharp edges.

clue_cards.name: Rice leaf
clue_cards.trick: Tiny waxy bumps arranged in grooves.
clue_cards.does: Water can't soak in, so drops roll along the grooves and off.

clue_cards.name: Eel
clue_cards.does: It slides through water and out of tight spots, and is very hard to grab.

predict.explain: Sticky things cling when they touch a surface directly. A thin layer of oil or wax in between keeps them apart, so they slide.

lab.title: The drop-race lab
lab.predict: Race a teaspoon of ketchup 20 cm down each ramp. Which surface will be fastest?
options: Plastic rubbed with an unlit candle
Plastic with a thin film of oil

tool.name: I Like, I Wish, What If
tool.intro: I Like, I Wish, What If is a way to give kind, useful feedback on a prototype, to a friend or to yourself. Today you'll learn all 3 parts.

parts.name: I like…
parts.what: Say one thing that works well.
parts.example: ✈️ I like how far it glides.
parts.starter: I like how the ketchup on Zane's ramp…

parts.name: I wish…
parts.what: Say one thing you'd like to be better.
parts.example: ✈️ I wish it didn't nose-dive at the end.

parts.name: What if…?
parts.what: Offer a new idea to try.
parts.example: ✈️ What if we folded the wing tips up a little?
parts.starter: What if we added a texture that…

sketch_checklist: I drew my surface as a close-up.
I labelled the surface, the slippery layer and the ketchup.
I showed what holds the slippery layer in place.

test.measure: seconds for a drop of ketchup to slide 20 cm
test.check_question: Clean check: how much ketchup is left on the ramp?

reflection.question: Which nature trick made your ketchup slide?
